subject: internet-packets
title: How a Message Crosses the Internet
summary: Your message is cut into small pieces that travel on their own.

cards.title: Your message gets chopped up
cards.text: When you send a photo to a friend, it does not travel in one piece. It is cut into lots of small pieces. Each piece can even take a different path!

cards.title: Packets
cards.text: The small pieces are called packets. Each packet has an address on it, like a letter in the mail. Computers along the way read the address and pass the packet closer to where it is going.

cards.title: Putting it back together
cards.text: Packets can arrive in a mixed-up order. The computer at the other end puts them back in the right order. If a packet gets lost, it is sent again.
cards.example: It is like mailing a puzzle one piece per envelope. Your friend sorts the pieces and asks for any missing one.

cards.title: Where it started
cards.text: In September 1969, a computer at UCLA, a college in California, became the first one on a new network called the ARPANET. By the end of that year, four computers were linked. That small network grew into the internet.

cards.title: Shared rules
cards.text: For computers to talk, they need to follow the same rules. In 1973, Bob Kahn and Vint Cerf began designing the rules that became TCP/IP. The internet still uses them today.

cards.question: Why do you think it is better to send small packets than one giant message?
nudges: What happens if one small piece is lost?

options.text: A small piece of a message with an address on it
options.why: Yes! Packets travel separately and get put back together.

options.text: A whole video in one piece

questions.q: What happens if a packet gets lost?

options.why: Right. The receiving computer can get a fresh copy.
No. One lost packet is just sent again.
The lost piece is sent again, so the message can be finished.

options.why: Yes. By the end of 1969, four computers were connected.
The first spot was UCLA in California.

sources.title: A Brief History of the Internet
sources.publisher: Internet Society (written by Internet pioneers including Cerf and Kahn)
sources.supports: Packet switching; the first ARPANET node at UCLA in September 1969 and four hosts by year-end; Kahn's open-architecture idea (1972); Cerf and Kahn's TCP; the split into TCP and IP; best-effort delivery and retransmission; the switch to TCP/IP on January 1, 1983; email's impact.

sources.title: Internet History, 1962 to 1992
